belt_squat.summary: The belt squat loads your hips through a belt instead of a bar on your back, so you can squat hard without spinal compression or shoulder mobility demands. It is a strong quad and glute builder, especially for lifters with back or shoulder limits.
belt_squat.musclesNote: The quads drive knee extension and the glutes drive the hips through as you stand. A narrower stance and more upright torso bias the quads; a wider stance and deeper hip hinge shift more work to the glutes and adductors.
setup: Stand on the platform and clip the belt around your hips, with the chain or strap centered between your legs.
Set your feet about shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly, under or just in front of the load point.
Hold the handles or rails lightly for balance, not to pull yourself up.
Stand up to release the lever or safety and take one step to settle your stance if the machine allows.
execution: Brace your trunk, then sit straight down, letting your knees travel forward over your toes.
Descend as deep as you can while keeping your heels down and your pelvis from tucking hard under.
Drive through your whole foot to stand, keeping the belt path vertical.
Use a controlled 2-3 second descent and stop just short of locking out to keep tension on the legs.

mistakes.fix: Keep your grip light; if you need to pull to stand, the load is too heavy.
Position the belt low on the hips and snug it before every set so it does not shift onto your lower back.
Drop the load and squat to a consistent depth you can repeat every rep, ideally thighs at or below parallel.

belt_squat.progression: Add reps within a range like 8-15 before adding plates, then go up 5-10 lb per side. Because there is no spinal limiter, it works well for higher-rep sets and for adding volume late in a leg session.

faq.q: Is the belt squat as good as a back squat?
faq.a: For building the quads and glutes it can be just as effective, since the legs do the same job. It does not train your trunk and upper back to support a bar, so powerlifters still need back squats for that skill.

faq.q: Is the belt squat good for people with back pain?
faq.a: Many people with cranky backs tolerate it well because nothing loads the spine from above. It is not a treatment, so if squatting in any form causes pain, get it assessed rather than pushing through.

smith_machine_squat.summary: The Smith machine squat runs the bar on fixed rails, removing balance so you can push your legs close to failure safely. Placing your feet slightly forward biases the quads; it suits beginners, solo lifters, and anyone chasing leg size.
smith_machine_squat.musclesNote: The quads extend the knee and the glutes extend the hip. Feet under the bar make it closer to a free squat; feet slightly forward lets you sit back more and changes knee and hip demand, while deeper squats increase glute contribution.
setup: Set the bar at upper-chest height and set the safety stops just below your bottom position.
Step under and place the bar across your upper traps, hands just outside shoulders.
Position your feet about shoulder-width, either directly under the bar or a few inches in front of it.
Stand up, rotate the bar to unhook it, and brace before the first rep.
execution: Take a breath, brace, and lower under control by bending knees and hips together.
Go as deep as you can while keeping your heels down and lower back neutral.
Drive up through your midfoot, keeping your chest up and knees tracking over your toes.
Re-brace at the top of each rep, and re-hook the bar by rotating the hooks when done.

mistakes.fix: Keep feet only a few inches ahead of the bar so your shins and back stay in a natural position instead of leaning back into the bar.
Always set the stops just below your lowest point so you can bail by simply sitting under the bar.
Reduce the load and use a full, consistent depth rather than chasing heavier partial reps.

smith_machine_squat.progression: Work up within a rep range like 6-12, then add 5-10 lb total once all sets hit the top. Bar weights vary between Smith machines, so compare your numbers only on the same machine.

faq.q: Is the Smith machine squat bad for your knees?
faq.a: Not inherently. It loads the knees like any squat, and placing your feet slightly forward can make it feel easier on some people's knees. Problems usually come from loading too fast or forcing an awkward foot position.

faq.q: Smith machine squat vs barbell squat: which is better?
faq.a: The barbell squat trains balance, bracing, and a transferable skill; the Smith squat lets you isolate the legs and train close to failure more safely. Use whichever fits your goal, or both.

smith_machine_bench.summary: The Smith machine bench press is a flat press on a fixed bar path, letting you train the chest and triceps hard without needing a spotter. It suits lifters training alone, those working around a shoulder that dislikes free-bar stabilization, or anyone pushing sets close to failure.
smith_machine_bench.musclesNote: The chest drives the arms forward and together, the triceps lock out the elbows, and the front delts assist throughout. A slightly wider grip biases the chest; a closer grip shifts more work to the triceps.
setup: Position the bench so the bar lowers to your lower chest, around nipple line.
Set the safety stops just above your chest at the bottom position.
Lie back with feet flat, shoulder blades pulled together and down, and a slight arch.
Grip the bar a little wider than shoulder-width and rotate it to unhook.
execution: Lower the bar under control for about 2 seconds to your lower chest, elbows around 45-70 degrees from your torso.
Touch lightly without bouncing, keeping your shoulder blades pinned.
Press straight up until your elbows are just short of locked.
Keep your feet planted and glutes on the bench for every rep.

mistakes.fix: Adjust the bench before loading so the bar meets your lower chest; the fixed path will not let you correct it mid-set.
Tuck your elbows slightly so your upper arms sit roughly 45-70 degrees from your sides to keep strain off the shoulders.
Retract and depress your shoulder blades before unracking and keep them there through the set.

smith_machine_bench.progression: Add reps in a 6-12 range, then increase by 5 lb total. The fixed path makes it easy to train safely near failure, so use it for hard sets once your barbell or dumbbell work is done.

faq.q: Is the Smith machine bench press effective for chest growth?
faq.a: Yes. The chest grows from hard, progressive sets through a full range, and the Smith machine provides that. It just does less to train the stabilizing skill of a free-bar bench.

faq.q: Why is my Smith bench weaker or stronger than my barbell bench?
faq.a: Smith bars can weigh less than 45 lb or be counterbalanced, and the fixed path removes balance demands. Treat it as its own lift and track it separately.

smith_machine_incline_press.summary: The Smith machine incline press is an incline bench press on a fixed bar path, aimed at the upper chest. It is a popular, low-skill way to load the upper pecs heavily and safely, and it suits anyone training alone or wanting a stable upper-chest press.
smith_machine_incline_press.musclesNote: The upper (clavicular) chest fibers do more work at an incline, with front delts contributing more than on a flat press. Triceps lock out the weight; steeper angles shift more emphasis to the shoulders.
setup: Set an adjustable bench at about 30 degrees; steeper turns it into more of a shoulder press.
Position the bench so the bar lowers to your upper chest just below the collarbones.
Set safeties just above your chest at the bottom.
Lie back with shoulder blades pinched and down, feet flat, and grip slightly wider than shoulder-width.
execution: Unhook the bar and lower it for about 2 seconds to your upper chest.
Keep elbows slightly tucked, under or a bit in front of the bar.
Press up until arms are nearly straight, keeping your upper back tight on the pad.
Pause briefly at the bottom without bouncing if you want to remove momentum.

mistakes.fix: Keep the incline around 15-30 degrees to keep the focus on the upper chest rather than the front delts.
Shift the bench so the bar lands on the upper chest; touching the sternum turns it into a flat press at an awkward angle.

mistakes.mistake: Lifting the hips off the bench
mistakes.fix: Keep your glutes down and drive through your feet without bridging up to flatten the angle.

smith_machine_incline_press.progression: Build reps in a 6-12 range before adding 5 lb. If shoulder discomfort appears, lower the incline or switch to dumbbells for a freer path.

faq.q: What angle is best for Smith machine incline press?
faq.a: Around 15-30 degrees works for most people. It is steep enough to bias the upper chest without turning the lift into a shoulder press.

faq.q: Smith incline vs dumbbell incline press?
faq.a: The Smith version is easier to load heavily and train safely to failure; dumbbells allow a more natural path and deeper stretch. Both build the upper chest well.

seated_leg_curl.summary: The seated leg curl isolates the hamstrings by bending the knee against resistance while your hips are flexed. That seated position stretches the hamstrings more than lying curls, making it one of the better machine choices for hamstring size, and it suits nearly everyone.
seated_leg_curl.musclesNote: The hamstrings flex the knee, and sitting with hips bent puts them in a lengthened position. Calves assist slightly; pointing toes down reduces calf involvement a little.
setup: Adjust the backrest so your knees line up with the machine's pivot point.
Set the lower pad just above your heels, on the back of your lower legs.
Lower the thigh pad so it presses firmly on your thighs just above the knees.
Hold the handles and sit tall against the backrest.
execution: Curl your heels down and back as far as the machine allows.
Squeeze briefly at the bottom of the curl.
Return slowly over 2-3 seconds until your knees are nearly straight.
Keep your hips pinned to the seat throughout.

mistakes.fix: Snug the thigh pad down so your hips cannot lift and your hamstrings stay working.
Use a full stretch at the top and a full curl at the bottom, reducing load if needed.
Control the return; letting the stack drop wastes the most productive part of the rep.

seated_leg_curl.progression: Work in a 8-15 rep range and add one plate on the stack once all sets reach the top. Small increments matter, so use add-on weights if the jumps are large.

faq.q: Seated vs lying leg curl: which is better?
faq.a: Seated curls train the hamstrings at a longer length because your hips are bent, which many lifters find more effective for growth. Both are useful, and using either consistently is what matters most.

faq.q: How many sets of seated leg curls should I do?
faq.a: Two to four hard sets per session, once or twice a week, is a solid starting point alongside a hip hinge like Romanian deadlifts.

standing_leg_curl.summary: The standing leg curl trains one hamstring at a time by curling the heel toward the glute while standing against a pad. It is a good way to fix side-to-side differences and get focused hamstring work, and suits anyone with access to the machine.
standing_leg_curl.musclesNote: The hamstrings flex the knee against the pad. Because the hip is fairly straight, the hamstrings work at a shorter length than in a seated curl, and the calf assists slightly.
setup: Adjust the machine so your knee lines up with the pivot point.
Place the roller pad just above your working heel on the back of the lower leg.
Rest your thigh against the front pad and hold the handles.
Stand tall on the support leg with a slight knee bend.
execution: Curl your heel up toward your glute without letting your hips move back.
Squeeze at the top for a moment.
Lower over 2-3 seconds until your knee is nearly straight.
Finish all reps on one leg, then switch.

mistakes.fix: Keep your thigh pressed into the front pad and lower the weight if your hips kick back.
Brace your abs and stay upright so the hamstring, not your back, moves the pad.
Lower to near-full extension on each rep instead of bouncing in the top half.

standing_leg_curl.progression: Use 8-15 reps per leg and add load once both legs hit the top of the range. Start each set with your weaker leg and match the reps on the stronger side.

faq.q: Is the standing leg curl good for hamstrings?
faq.a: Yes, it is a direct hamstring isolation exercise and the single-leg setup helps even out imbalances. Pair it with a hinge movement for complete hamstring training.

faq.q: Standing leg curl vs seated leg curl?
faq.a: Seated curls train the hamstrings in a more stretched position; standing curls work one leg at a time. Either works well, and you can rotate them between training blocks.

glute_drive_machine.summary: The glute drive machine is a plate- or stack-loaded hip thrust: you lean back on a pad, a belt or pad sits across your hips, and you drive them up. It loads the glutes heavily without setting up a barbell, and suits anyone wanting a simple, stable hip thrust.
glute_drive_machine.musclesNote: The glutes extend the hip and are most loaded near the top of the movement. The hamstrings assist with hip extension; feet farther out increases their contribution, while feet closer keeps the glutes in focus.
setup: Sit on the seat with your upper back against the back pad, around your shoulder blades.
Position the hip belt or pad across your hip crease, not your stomach.
Place your feet flat, about hip-width, so your shins are vertical at the top.
Hold the handles and tuck your chin slightly.
execution: Drive through your heels and push your hips up until your torso and thighs form a straight line.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top for a second without arching your lower back.
Lower under control until your hips drop a few inches below the start of tension.
Keep your ribs down and gaze forward to avoid overextending.

mistakes.mistake: Arching the lower back at the top
mistakes.fix: Finish with a slight posterior pelvic tilt and ribs down so the glutes, not the spine, complete the lockout.
Bring your feet in until shins are vertical at the top if you mostly feel your hamstrings.
Pause briefly at the top and control the lowering instead of rebounding off the bottom.

glute_drive_machine.progression: Work up in an 8-15 rep range, adding plates once you can hold a clean top squeeze on every rep. Heavier loads are fine as long as the lockout stays crisp.

faq.q: Is the glute drive machine as good as a barbell hip thrust?
faq.a: For glute development it does the same job and is faster to set up and more comfortable on the hips. The barbell version is more portable and easier to load very heavily in some gyms.

faq.q: Why do I feel the glute drive in my hamstrings or back?
faq.a: Hamstrings usually mean your feet are too far out; back means you are arching at the top. Adjust foot position and finish with ribs down.

hip_abductor_machine.summary: The hip abductor machine has you sit and push your knees outward against pads, training the muscles on the side of the hip. It is a simple, low-skill way to add direct glute medius work and suits anyone after more rounded glutes or extra hip stability work.
hip_abductor_machine.musclesNote: The glute medius and minimus, plus the upper glute max, abduct the hip by pushing the thighs apart. Leaning forward from the hips tends to bring in more glute max; sitting upright keeps the focus on the glute medius.
setup: Set the starting width so the pads sit just outside your knees with your legs together or slightly apart.
Sit with your back against the pad, or lean forward slightly if targeting the glute max.
Place your feet on the footrests and hold the handles.
Brace lightly so your torso does not rock.
execution: Push your knees out against the pads as far as you can control.
Pause for a moment at the widest point.
Return slowly over 2 seconds, stopping before the stack touches down.
Keep your hips on the seat and avoid jerking the pads open.

mistakes.fix: Slow the lowering and pause at the outer position so the muscle, not a swing, moves the weight.
Reduce load and use the full opening range you can control.
Keep your hips planted; if you rise up or rock, the weight is too heavy.

hip_abductor_machine.progression: These respond well to moderate-to-high reps, around 12-20. Add a plate when you can complete all sets at the top of the range with a clean pause.

faq.q: Does the hip abductor machine build glutes?
faq.a: It trains the glute medius and upper glutes directly, which adds to the side and upper shape of the hips. It works best alongside heavy hip extension work like hip thrusts or squats.

faq.q: Should I lean forward on the abductor machine?
faq.a: Leaning forward shifts some emphasis toward the glute max, while upright focuses on the glute medius. Both are valid; pick based on what you want to target.

hip_adductor_machine.summary: The hip adductor machine has you sit and squeeze your legs together against pads, training the inner thigh muscles. Strong adductors help in squats and deadlifts and support hip health, so it suits both lifters and general gym-goers.
hip_adductor_machine.musclesNote: The adductors pull the thighs toward the midline and also assist hip extension from a deep squat. Wider starting positions train them in a more stretched position.
setup: Set the starting width so you feel a comfortable stretch in your inner thighs, not a strain.
Sit upright with your back against the pad.
Place the pads on the inside of your knees and feet on the footrests.
Hold the handles and brace lightly.
execution: Squeeze your knees together until the pads meet or nearly meet.
Pause briefly at the closed position.
Open slowly over 2-3 seconds back to the stretched position.
Keep the stack from slamming between reps.

mistakes.fix: Build into wider starting positions gradually over a few weeks rather than forcing a big stretch on day one.
Control the opening phase; the stretched position is where much of the work happens.
Close the pads fully on each rep and lower the weight if you cannot.

hip_adductor_machine.progression: Use 10-20 reps and add load once you can control the full range. Increase the starting width gradually as your flexibility allows.

faq.q: Is the adductor machine worth doing?
faq.a: Yes. The adductors are a large muscle group that contributes to squatting and hip stability, and direct work is an easy way to strengthen them.

faq.q: Does the adductor machine burn inner thigh fat?
faq.a: No, you cannot spot-reduce fat. It builds the inner thigh muscles; fat loss comes from overall diet and activity.

glute_kickback_machine.summary: The glute kickback machine trains one glute at a time by driving the leg back against a pad or plate while your torso is supported. It is an isolation finisher that suits lifters wanting extra glute volume or working on a side-to-side imbalance.
glute_kickback_machine.musclesNote: The glute max extends the hip as the leg drives back. Hamstrings assist somewhat; keeping the knee bent reduces their involvement and keeps the focus on the glutes.
setup: Adjust the chest or forearm pad so your torso is supported and your hips are square.
Place the working foot on the platform or the pad against the back of your heel or thigh, as the machine dictates.
Stand firmly on the support leg with a soft knee.
Brace your abs and keep your back flat.
execution: Drive the working leg back and up by squeezing your glute.
Stop when your hip is fully extended, without arching your lower back.
Hold for a moment, then return slowly until you feel a stretch in the glute.
Complete all reps on one side, then switch.

mistakes.fix: Stop the kick at full hip extension and keep your ribs down so the spine does not take over.
Keep both hip bones facing the machine for the whole rep.
Control both directions and pause at the top instead of kicking for momentum.

glute_kickback_machine.progression: Work 10-20 reps per side and add load when both sides reach the top of the range with a clean pause. Do it after heavier compound glute work.

faq.q: Are glute kickbacks effective?
faq.a: Yes, as an isolation exercise they add focused glute work. They are best used alongside heavier movements like hip thrusts, squats, or lunges rather than in place of them.

faq.q: How many sets of glute kickbacks should I do?
faq.a: Two to three sets per side at the end of a lower-body session is plenty for most people.

pec_deck.summary: The pec deck is a seated machine fly where you bring padded arms or handles together in front of your chest. It isolates the chest with constant tension and little shoulder stabilization demand, making it a good finisher for anyone after chest size.
pec_deck.musclesNote: The chest pulls the upper arms across the body (horizontal adduction). The front delts assist slightly, but with the elbows held in a fixed slight bend the triceps do very little.
setup: Adjust the seat so the handles are at or just below shoulder height.
Set the arms so you feel a stretch in the chest at the start without your shoulders pushing past comfort.
Sit with your back on the pad, chest up, and shoulder blades pulled back.
Grip the handles or place your forearms on the pads with a slight elbow bend.
execution: Bring your arms together in a wide arc, leading with your elbows.
Squeeze your chest when the handles meet in front of you.
Return slowly over 2-3 seconds to a comfortable stretch.
Keep your shoulders down and back throughout.

mistakes.fix: Keep your chest up and shoulder blades back so the chest does the work, not the front delts.
Set the start position to a firm stretch you can control, not a range that pulls at the front of the shoulder.
Keep the elbow angle fixed and move in an arc rather than bending and straightening the arms.

pec_deck.progression: Use 10-15 reps and add a plate when all sets hit the top. Because it is an isolation lift, prioritize a controlled stretch and squeeze over heavy load.

faq.q: Pec deck vs cable fly: which is better?
faq.a: Both isolate the chest well. The pec deck is more stable and easier to learn; cables allow more angle options. Use whichever you can feel and progress best.

faq.q: Should I do pec deck before or after bench press?
faq.a: Usually after, as a finisher. Some lifters use a light set or two before pressing to warm up the chest.

rear_delt_machine.summary: The rear delt machine, or reverse pec deck, has you face the pad and sweep your arms back to train the rear shoulders and upper back. It is one of the easiest ways to load the rear delts directly and suits anyone wanting better shoulder balance and posture.
rear_delt_machine.musclesNote: The rear delts pull the arms back horizontally, with the middle traps and rhomboids squeezing the shoulder blades toward the end. Keeping the shoulder blades from fully pinching keeps more focus on the rear delts.
setup: Sit facing the pad with your chest against it.
Adjust the seat so the handles are at shoulder height.
Set the handles so your arms start straight in front of you.
Use a neutral or palms-down grip with a slight elbow bend.
execution: Sweep your arms back and out in a wide arc until they are in line with your body.
Lead with your elbows and keep the elbow angle fixed.
Pause briefly, then return slowly over 2 seconds.
Keep your chest on the pad and avoid shrugging.

mistakes.fix: Keep your shoulders down away from your ears so the traps do not take over.
Use a lighter weight you can control; rear delts are small and respond well to higher reps.
Keep the elbow angle constant so it stays a fly, not a row.

rear_delt_machine.progression: Use 12-20 reps and add a small amount of weight only when all sets are clean. Volume and consistency matter more than heavy loads here.

faq.q: Does the reverse pec deck work traps?
faq.a: Yes, the middle traps and rhomboids help pull the shoulder blades together near the end. The rear delts are still the main target.

faq.q: How often should I train rear delts?
faq.a: Two to three times per week with a few sets each is common, since rear delts recover quickly and respond well to frequent, moderate work.

machine_lateral_raise.summary: The machine lateral raise lifts your arms out to the sides against padded levers, isolating the side delts. It provides consistent tension through the range and suits anyone wanting wider shoulders without the swinging that often creeps into dumbbell raises.
machine_lateral_raise.musclesNote: The side delts lift the arm away from the body. The upper traps assist when you raise past shoulder height or shrug, so stopping near shoulder level keeps the focus on the delts.
setup: Adjust the seat so the machine's pivot lines up with your shoulder joint.
Sit with your chest against the pad or back against the support, depending on the machine.
Place the outside of your arms or elbows against the pads with a slight bend.
Hold the handles lightly.
execution: Raise your arms out to the sides, leading with your elbows.
Stop at or just above shoulder height.
Pause, then lower slowly over 2-3 seconds.
Keep your shoulders down and avoid shrugging.

mistakes.fix: Keep your shoulders depressed and stop at shoulder height so the traps do not take over.
Adjust the seat height until the machine's axis matches your shoulder joint.
Control the lowering instead of letting the stack fall.

machine_lateral_raise.progression: Use 12-20 reps and add the smallest increment available once all sets are clean. Side delts recover well, so frequent sessions work.

faq.q: Machine vs dumbbell lateral raise?
faq.a: The machine gives steady tension and is harder to cheat on; dumbbells are more available and adjustable. Both build side delts well.

faq.q: How many sets of lateral raises for wider shoulders?
faq.a: Around 6-12 sets per week across two or three sessions is a reasonable range for most lifters.

machine_shoulder_press.summary: The machine shoulder press is a seated overhead press on a guided path, so you can push the front delts and triceps close to failure without balancing a bar or dumbbells. It suits beginners, lifters training alone, and anyone whose shoulders prefer a fixed, supported press.
machine_shoulder_press.musclesNote: The front delts drive the arms up, the triceps finish the lockout, and the side delts help more as the elbows flare out to the sides. Machines with a neutral (palms-in) grip tend to keep elbows forward and feel easier on cranky shoulders.
setup: Adjust the seat so the handles start at or just below shoulder height; too low overstretches the shoulder.
Sit with your hips and upper back against the pad, feet flat and a little wider than hips.
Grip the handles with wrists straight and stacked over your elbows.
Brace your abs so your ribs stay down against the pad.
execution: Press up and slightly back along the machine's path until your elbows are just short of locked.
Keep your head and upper back on the pad; do not crane your neck forward.
Lower over 2-3 seconds until the handles are back at shoulder level.
Reset your brace at the bottom instead of bouncing out of it.

mistakes.fix: Keep your ribs down and lower back near the pad; if you have to arch to finish a rep, drop the weight.
Bring the handles all the way down to shoulder height each rep, using a lighter load if needed.
Raise the seat so the starting position is not a deep, uncomfortable stretch at the front of the shoulder.

machine_shoulder_press.progression: Work in a 6-12 rep range and add one plate or pin once every set reaches the top of the range. When the machine stops feeling challenging relative to your free-weight work, use it for the back-off or high-rep sets.

faq.q: Is the machine shoulder press good for building shoulders?
faq.a: Yes. It loads the front delts and triceps through a stable path, which makes it easy to train hard and add weight over time. Add lateral raises if you also want to target the side delts directly.

faq.q: Machine shoulder press vs dumbbell shoulder press?
faq.a: The machine is more stable, quicker to load, and safer to take to failure; dumbbells demand more stabilization and let each arm find its own path. Both build the shoulders, so choose based on comfort and equipment.

assisted_pull_up.summary: The assisted pull-up machine uses a counterweight to offset part of your bodyweight, so you can do full-range pull-ups before you can manage them unassisted. It is the most direct way for beginners to build toward real pull-ups.
assisted_pull_up.musclesNote: The lats pull your upper arms down to your sides and the biceps bend the elbows. A wider overhand grip leans more on the lats and upper back, while a narrow or underhand (chin-up) grip brings in more biceps.
setup: Pick the assistance: on most machines, more weight on the stack means more help, so start heavier and reduce it.
Step up and grip the handles slightly wider than shoulder-width, then place your knees or feet on the pad or platform.
Lower yourself to a full hang with arms straight.
Pull your shoulders down slightly away from your ears before the first rep.
execution: Drive your elbows down toward your back pockets and pull until your chin clears the handles.
Keep your chest up and your body still; no kicking or swinging.
Lower over 2-3 seconds to a full hang with straight arms.
Use the same full range on every rep.

mistakes.fix: Use the least help that still lets you reach your rep target with full range, and reduce it as soon as you exceed that target.

mistakes.mistake: Stopping short of a full hang
mistakes.fix: Straighten your arms fully at the bottom, because the bottom position is where unassisted pull-ups are hardest.
Start each rep by drawing the shoulders down, then pull with the elbows so the traps do not take over.

assisted_pull_up.progression: Once you hit 8-12 clean reps, reduce the assistance by one plate or pin. When you need only a small amount of help, start practicing unassisted reps or slow negatives at the start of the session.

faq.q: Does the assisted pull-up machine help you do real pull-ups?
faq.a: Yes. It trains the same movement through the same range, and gradually reducing the assistance builds the strength to lift your full bodyweight. Pair it with slow negatives once you are close.

faq.q: Assisted pull-up vs lat pulldown: which is better?
faq.a: Both build the lats well. The assisted pull-up is closer to a real pull-up because your body moves around a fixed bar, while the pulldown is easier to adjust in small steps. Many people use both.

assisted_dip.summary: The assisted dip machine uses a counterweight to support part of your bodyweight while you lower and press yourself between parallel handles. It builds the triceps, lower chest, and front delts, and suits anyone working toward bodyweight dips or wanting dips without the full load.
assisted_dip.musclesNote: The triceps straighten the elbows and do much of the work, the lower chest pushes the arms down and forward, and the front delts assist. Leaning your torso forward shifts work toward the chest; staying upright biases the triceps.
setup: Set the assistance: more weight on the stack typically means more help.
Grip the parallel handles with hands about shoulder-width, just outside your hips.
Kneel or stand on the pad and press up to straight arms.
Set your shoulders down and back, chest up.
execution: Lower slowly by bending your elbows, keeping them pointed mostly back rather than flared out.
Stop when your upper arms are about parallel to the floor or slightly below, as far as your shoulders tolerate.
Press back up until your elbows are straight.
Use a 2-3 second descent and no bounce at the bottom.

mistakes.fix: Stop around parallel unless deeper feels fine on your shoulders; forcing extra depth adds strain without much benefit.
Keep your chest up and shoulders pulled back so the front of the shoulder is not hanging on the joint.
Keep the elbows tracking back along your sides to keep the triceps working and the shoulders comfortable.

assisted_dip.progression: When you reach about 12 controlled reps, reduce the assistance one step. Once you can do several reps with little help, try bodyweight dips on parallel bars.

faq.q: Are assisted dips good for triceps?
faq.a: Yes. The triceps work through a long range under meaningful load, especially with an upright torso. They make a strong base exercise before isolation work like pushdowns.

faq.q: Are dips bad for your shoulders?
faq.a: Most people tolerate dips well with controlled depth and the shoulders kept back. If the front of your shoulder hurts, reduce depth or swap to a press that feels better.

machine_preacher_curl.summary: The machine preacher curl braces your upper arms on an angled pad while you curl handles along a guided path. Because you cannot swing, it isolates the biceps well and loads them hard near the stretched bottom position, making it a good choice for arm growth at any level.
machine_preacher_curl.musclesNote: The biceps bend the elbow, with the brachialis assisting strongly. The pad holds the upper arm in front of the body, which removes shoulder involvement and makes the bottom of the rep the hardest part.
setup: Adjust the seat so your armpits sit snug against the top of the pad.
Lay the backs of your upper arms flat on the pad with elbows lined up with the machine's pivot.
Grip the handles palms up, wrists straight.
Sit tall with your chest close to the pad.
execution: Curl the handles up until your forearms are near vertical, squeezing the biceps.
Keep your upper arms and elbows in contact with the pad throughout.
Lower over 2-3 seconds until your elbows are almost straight.
Reverse smoothly at the bottom without bouncing out of the stretch.

mistakes.fix: Keep the backs of your arms pressed into the pad; if they lift, the weight is too heavy.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping the bottom of the rep
mistakes.fix: Lower until your arms are nearly straight, because the stretched position is where this exercise is most useful.
Raise the seat so your armpits reach the top of the pad and your elbows match the pivot.

machine_preacher_curl.progression: Work in 8-15 reps and add the smallest increment once every set reaches the top. If you plateau, slow the lowering phase before adding more load.

faq.q: Are machine preacher curls good for biceps?
faq.a: Yes. They isolate the biceps, prevent cheating, and load the muscle in its stretched position, which makes them a reliable growth exercise.

faq.q: Preacher curl vs standing curl: which is better?
faq.a: Preacher curls emphasize the bottom of the range and limit body swing; standing curls allow heavier loads and challenge the top more. Using both across a program covers the whole range.

machine_tricep_extension.summary: The machine tricep extension fixes your upper arms on a pad while you straighten your elbows against a guided lever. It isolates the triceps with a stable, repeatable path and suits anyone wanting direct arm work, especially if free-weight extensions bother the elbows.
machine_tricep_extension.musclesNote: All three triceps heads straighten the elbow. Machines that set your arms out in front or overhead stretch the long head more, giving it a bigger share of the work.
setup: Adjust the seat so your elbows line up with the machine's pivot point.
Rest the backs of your upper arms on the pad.
Grip the handles with wrists straight.
Sit tall with your back against the support and feet planted.
execution: Push the handles down or forward until your elbows are straight.
Squeeze the triceps at lockout for a moment.
Return over 2-3 seconds until your elbows are well bent and the triceps feel stretched.
Keep your upper arms still; only the forearms move.

mistakes.fix: Keep your upper arms planted on the pad so the shoulders and chest do not help push.
Adjust the seat so your elbows line up with the machine's axis; misalignment strains the elbow and shortens the range.
Use the full range from a deep bend to full lockout, lowering the weight if needed.

machine_tricep_extension.progression: Use 10-15 reps and add one pin once all sets hit the top. If your elbows feel achy, stay in higher reps rather than pushing heavy loads.

faq.q: Is the tricep extension machine effective?
faq.a: Yes. It isolates the triceps and keeps tension steady through the rep, making it a good complement to pressing movements.

faq.q: Tricep machine vs cable pushdown?
faq.a: Both isolate the triceps. The machine is more stable and repeatable; cables give more angle and attachment options. Pick the one that feels best on your elbows.

machine_crunch.summary: The machine ab crunch has you curl your torso forward against a weighted pad or handles, letting you load the abs and track progress like any other lift. It suits anyone who wants stronger abs and finds bodyweight crunches too easy to progress.
machine_crunch.musclesNote: The rectus abdominis flexes the spine, pulling the ribs toward the pelvis, with the obliques assisting. If you hinge at the hips instead of rounding the spine, the hip flexors take over much of the work.
setup: Adjust the seat so the pads or handles sit at your upper chest or shoulders.
Hook your feet under the rollers or place them on the footrest.
Grip the handles lightly or set your arms on the pads.
Sit tall against the backpad to start.
execution: Exhale and curl your ribs down toward your hips, rounding your spine.
Squeeze your abs at the bottom for a moment.
Return over 2 seconds until your torso is upright and the abs are stretched.
Move through your spine; your arms just hold position.

mistakes.fix: Keep your arms passive and let your abs curl you forward.
Think of shortening the distance between ribs and pelvis instead of folding forward from the hips.
Control both directions to keep tension on the abs.

machine_crunch.progression: Use 10-20 reps and add one pin once all sets hit the top. Train abs two or three times a week with a few hard sets rather than endless light reps.

faq.q: Is the ab crunch machine effective?
faq.a: Yes. It lets you add resistance and progress over time, which helps build ab strength and thickness.

faq.q: Will crunches give me a six-pack?
faq.a: Crunches strengthen and build the abs, but whether they are visible depends mostly on body fat, which comes down to diet and overall activity.

torso_rotation_machine.summary: The torso rotation machine locks your hips in place while you rotate your upper body against resistance. It trains the obliques and rotational strength in a controlled way, and suits athletes in rotational sports or anyone wanting balanced core work.
torso_rotation_machine.musclesNote: The obliques do most of the work, turning the ribcage relative to the pelvis, while the rest of the abs stabilize. Locking the hips keeps the work in the trunk instead of letting the hips spin.
setup: Adjust the seat and pads so your hips and legs are locked in place.
Set the range limiter to a comfortable rotation, not your maximum twist.
Grip the handles or place your arms on the pads.
Sit tall with a neutral spine.
execution: Rotate your torso away from the start, moving your ribs and shoulders together.
Keep your hips still and your spine tall, without slumping.
Return slowly over 2 seconds to the start.
Complete all reps to one side, then switch.

mistakes.fix: Use a moderate load you can turn smoothly through the whole range.
Rotate under control rather than whipping the handles.
Keep the rotation within a range that feels comfortable, especially if your back is sensitive.

torso_rotation_machine.progression: Use 10-15 reps per side and add weight in small steps. Prioritize smooth control over load.

faq.q: Is the torso rotation machine bad for your back?
faq.a: Not for most people when used with moderate weight and controlled range. If rotating under load aggravates your back, try anti-rotation work like Pallof presses instead.

faq.q: Does the torso rotation machine slim the waist?
faq.a: No exercise burns fat from one spot. It strengthens the obliques; waist size depends mostly on overall body fat.

cable_row_wide_grip.summary: The wide grip cable row is a seated row with a wide bar, pulling toward the lower chest with elbows out. It biases the upper back and rear delts more than close-grip rows and suits anyone wanting thicker upper back and better posture.
cable_row_wide_grip.musclesNote: With elbows flared, the rear delts, rhomboids, and middle traps do more of the work, while the lats still contribute. The biceps assist with elbow bend.
setup: Attach a wide bar and sit with your feet on the platform, knees slightly bent.
Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width, palms down.
Sit tall with a neutral spine and the cable taut.
Start with your arms straight and shoulders reaching slightly forward.
execution: Pull the bar toward your lower chest, with elbows flared about 45-70 degrees from your torso.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end.
Return slowly over 2 seconds, letting your shoulders reach forward.
Keep your torso mostly still; a small lean is fine.

mistakes.fix: Keep your torso near upright and reduce the weight if you rock back.
Keep your shoulders down as you pull so the upper traps do not take over.
Let the shoulder blades spread at the start and squeeze together at the end of each rep.

cable_row_wide_grip.progression: Work in 8-15 reps and add one pin when all sets hit the top. Keep the pull clean before adding weight.

faq.q: Wide grip vs close grip cable row?
faq.a: Wide grip with elbows out biases the upper back and rear delts; close grip with elbows tucked biases the lats. Both build the back.

faq.q: Is the wide grip row good for rear delts?
faq.a: Yes. Flaring the elbows brings in more rear delt work than a close-grip row.

cable_row_close_grip.summary: The close grip cable row uses a V-handle or narrow grip to pull toward your lower ribs. It emphasizes the lats and mid-back and is a reliable staple back exercise for most lifters.
cable_row_close_grip.musclesNote: The lats pull the arms back close to your sides, while the rhomboids and mid traps squeeze the shoulder blades. The biceps assist with elbow flexion.
setup: Attach a V-handle and sit with your feet on the platform, knees slightly bent.
Grip the handle with palms facing each other.
Sit tall with a neutral spine.
Start with arms straight and shoulders reaching slightly forward.
execution: Pull the handle toward your lower ribs, elbows close to your sides.
Squeeze your back at the end of the pull.
Return slowly over 2 seconds to a full stretch.
Keep your torso steady; avoid rocking.

mistakes.fix: Keep your torso steady and let your back do the pulling.
Keep a neutral spine and bend slightly at the hips if you need more reach.
Let your arms fully extend and your shoulder blades spread between reps.

cable_row_close_grip.progression: Use 8-15 reps and add weight when you hit the top of the range. Keep form strict as you progress.

faq.q: Is the close grip row good for lats?
faq.a: Yes. Keeping the elbows tight to your body emphasizes the lats.

faq.q: How many sets of rows should I do?
faq.a: Three to four sets per session is common, depending on your total weekly back volume.

close_grip_lat_pulldown.summary: The close grip lat pulldown uses a narrow neutral-grip handle to pull toward your upper chest with elbows tucked. It often allows a longer range and heavier loads than a wide grip, and suits anyone building lat size or working toward pull-ups.
close_grip_lat_pulldown.musclesNote: The lats pull the upper arms down and back toward the hips, which a tucked-elbow path suits well. The biceps and brachialis assist more than on a wide overhand grip because the neutral grip is a strong elbow-flexing position.
setup: Attach a V-bar or close neutral-grip handle to the high pulley.
Set the thigh pad so your legs are locked in snugly.
Grab the handle with palms facing each other and sit down with arms fully extended.
Lean back slightly, about 10-20 degrees, with your chest up.
execution: Start by pulling your shoulders down, then drive your elbows down toward your hips.
Pull until the handle reaches your upper chest, with elbows close to your sides.
Pause briefly, then let the handle rise over 2-3 seconds until your arms are straight and lats stretched.
Keep the torso angle fixed; do not rock back to start each rep.

mistakes.fix: Hold a small, fixed lean; swinging back to 45 degrees turns it into a row and lets momentum lift the weight.
Think about driving the elbows down rather than curling the handle with your hands.
Let your arms straighten fully and shoulders rise slightly at the top of each rep.

close_grip_lat_pulldown.progression: Work in 8-12 reps and add one pin once all sets reach the top with a controlled stretch. Rotate with wide-grip pulldowns or pull-ups between training blocks for variety.

faq.q: Close grip vs wide grip lat pulldown: which is better?
faq.a: Neither is strictly better. Close grip usually allows a longer range and heavier loads with more arm help; wide grip brings in more upper back. Both build the lats.

faq.q: Does the close grip pulldown work biceps?
faq.a: Yes, the biceps assist in bending the elbows, more so than on a wide grip. It is still primarily a back exercise, so do separate curls if arm size is a goal.

straight_arm_pulldown.summary: The straight arm pulldown has you sweep a bar or rope from overhead down to your thighs with your elbows locked in a slight bend. It trains the lats with almost no biceps involvement, making it useful for learning to feel your lats and as a finisher after rows and pulldowns.
straight_arm_pulldown.musclesNote: The lats pull the arms down from overhead to the hips (shoulder extension). With the elbows fixed the biceps barely help; the long head of the triceps and the rear delts assist a little.
setup: Attach a straight bar or rope to a high pulley.
Stand an arm's length or so back, feet hip-width, knees soft.
Grip the handle with arms extended and a slight, fixed bend at the elbows.
Hinge forward 20-30 degrees at the hips with a flat back so the cable lines up with your arms.
execution: Pull the handle down in an arc by driving your arms toward your thighs.
Keep the elbow angle fixed the whole rep.
Squeeze your lats when your hands reach your thighs.
Let the handle rise over 2-3 seconds until your arms are overhead and the lats are stretched.

mistakes.fix: Hold a fixed elbow angle; bending and straightening turns it into a tricep pushdown.
Keep your hip hinge angle steady so the lats, not body movement, move the weight.
Use a load you can control through the full arc; this lift works best with moderate weight and a strong squeeze.

straight_arm_pulldown.progression: Use 10-15 reps and add one pin once you can hold the bottom squeeze on every rep. It works well as a lighter primer before heavy back work or a finisher after it.

faq.q: What muscles does the straight arm pulldown work?
faq.a: It mainly works the lats, with small help from the rear delts and the long head of the triceps. The biceps do very little because the elbows do not bend.

faq.q: Rope or bar for straight arm pulldowns?
faq.a: A rope lets your hands come apart and slightly behind your body at the bottom, which some people feel more in the lats. A bar is simpler and more stable. Use whichever you feel better.

cable_chest_press.summary: The cable chest press uses two cable handles, so tension stays on the chest through the whole rep and each arm works independently. It suits lifters wanting a shoulder-friendly press or extra chest volume after heavier pressing.
cable_chest_press.musclesNote: The chest pushes the arms forward and together, the triceps straighten the elbows, and the front delts assist. Standing versions also make the core work to stop you being pulled backward.
setup: Set both pulleys at about chest height, or slightly below.
Grab the handles and step forward into a split stance until the weight lifts off the stack.
Bring the handles beside your chest, elbows slightly below shoulder height.
Brace your abs and lean forward a little into the cables.
execution: Press the handles forward and slightly inward until your arms are nearly straight.
Let your hands come close together at the end without clanking the handles.
Return over 2-3 seconds until your hands are beside your chest and you feel a stretch.
Keep your torso still; your arms move, not your body.

mistakes.fix: Use a staggered stance with a firm brace, and reduce the load if the cables drag you backward.
Bring the handles back to chest level each rep to keep the full stretch.
Keep elbows a bit below shoulder level to keep strain off the front of the shoulders.

cable_chest_press.progression: Work in 8-15 reps, adding a pin when all sets reach the top. Standing presses are limited by balance, so once loading gets awkward, do the same press seated or on a bench.

faq.q: Is the cable chest press good for building chest?
faq.a: Yes. It loads the chest through a full range with steady tension. It is not ideal for very heavy loads, so most lifters pair it with a bench or machine press.

faq.q: Cable chest press vs bench press?
faq.a: The bench press lets you lift much heavier and progress strength more easily. The cable press offers constant tension and a freer path that some shoulders prefer.

incline_cable_fly.summary: The incline cable fly is done on an incline bench set between two low pulleys, sweeping the handles together over your upper chest. It isolates the upper chest with tension throughout the arc, and suits lifters whose upper chest lags behind.
incline_cable_fly.musclesNote: The chest pulls the arms across the body, and the incline angle shifts emphasis to the upper (clavicular) fibers. The front delts assist more as the bench gets steeper.
setup: Set an incline bench at 30 degrees or less between two low pulleys.
Grab a handle in each hand and lie back with your feet flat.
Start with arms out wide, palms facing up and in, and a slight fixed elbow bend.
Pull your shoulder blades back and down into the bench.
execution: Sweep the handles up and together in an arc until they meet above your upper chest.
Squeeze your chest at the top without letting your shoulders lift off the bench.
Lower over 2-3 seconds until your hands are roughly level with the bench and your chest is stretched.
Keep the elbow angle fixed throughout.

mistakes.fix: Keep a fixed, slight elbow bend instead of bending and straightening the arms.
Stop where you feel a solid chest stretch, not a pull at the front of the shoulder.
Keep the angle at about 30 degrees or lower to keep the chest, not the delts, doing the work.

incline_cable_fly.progression: Use 10-15 reps and add one pin when all sets reach the top with a controlled stretch. Program it after your main presses.

faq.q: Does the incline cable fly target the upper chest?
faq.a: Yes. The incline shifts emphasis toward the upper chest fibers, and cables keep tension on them at the top, where dumbbell flys go slack.

faq.q: Incline cable fly vs incline dumbbell press?
faq.a: The press builds strength and lets you lift heavier with triceps help; the fly isolates the chest. Doing both is a common, effective pairing.

high_cable_fly.summary: The high to low cable fly brings the handles from high pulleys down and together in front of your lower chest or upper abs. It emphasizes the lower chest with constant tension and suits anyone wanting a finisher that complements flat and incline pressing.
high_cable_fly.musclesNote: The chest pulls the arms down and across the body; the downward path favors the lower (sternal) fibers. The front delts assist, and the core braces to keep you stable.
setup: Set both pulleys above head height.
Grab a handle in each hand and step forward into a staggered stance until the weight lifts.
Lean forward slightly from the hips with chest up.
Start with your arms out wide and a slight fixed bend in the elbows.
execution: Sweep your hands down and together in an arc, finishing in front of your lower chest.
Squeeze your chest hard where your hands meet.
Return over 2-3 seconds until you feel a stretch across the chest.
Keep the elbow angle fixed and your torso still.

mistakes.fix: Lock in a slight elbow bend so the movement stays a fly, not a press.
Keep your chest up and shoulders back, especially at the bottom of the arc.
Keep your stance and lean fixed so your chest, not body momentum, moves the handles.

high_cable_fly.progression: Use 10-15 reps and add one pin once all sets hit the top. Keep it as a finisher rather than chasing heavy loads.

faq.q: Does the high to low cable fly work the lower chest?
faq.a: Yes. The downward arc lines up with the lower chest fibers, so it emphasizes that area while still training the whole chest.

faq.q: How many sets of high to low cable flys should I do?
faq.a: Two to four sets of 10-15 reps after your pressing is plenty for most people.

low_cable_fly.summary: The low to high cable fly sweeps the handles from low pulleys up and together in front of your upper chest. It emphasizes the upper chest with tension at the top of the arc, and suits anyone wanting an upper-chest finisher without needing a bench.
low_cable_fly.musclesNote: The upper (clavicular) chest fibers pull the arms up and across the body, with the front delts assisting noticeably. Keeping the shoulders down stops the delts from taking over.
setup: Set both pulleys at the lowest position.
Grab a handle in each hand and step forward into a staggered stance until the weight lifts.
Stand tall with arms down and slightly behind your hips, palms facing forward, elbows slightly bent.
Brace your abs and pull your shoulders back.
execution: Sweep the handles up and inward until they meet at upper-chest or chin height.
Squeeze your upper chest at the top without shrugging.
Lower over 2-3 seconds back to the start, feeling a stretch across your chest.
Keep the elbow angle fixed throughout.

mistakes.fix: Keep your shoulders down and back and stop at upper-chest height instead of raising the arms higher.
Use a weight you can control; heavier loads usually turn the fly into a front raise.
Hold a slight, fixed elbow bend so the arms move in an arc.

low_cable_fly.progression: Use 12-15 reps and add one pin once all sets reach the top with a clean squeeze. Pair it with incline pressing for a complete upper-chest workout.

faq.q: Does the low to high cable fly work the upper chest?
faq.a: Yes. The upward arc lines up with the upper chest fibers, making it a good isolation option for that area.

faq.q: Low to high vs high to low cable fly?
faq.a: Low to high emphasizes the upper chest; high to low emphasizes the lower chest. Many lifters use both across the week.
